Mitchell Player

Bassist Mitchell Player is a longtime resident of New Orleans and a passionate advocate for the importance of the city’s unique culture. Mitchell has performed with some of the city’s best known artists, including Leroy Jones and Michael White.
Mitchell was interviewed in Clinton, New York, on November 8, 2012, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and we are in the Jazz Archive at Hamilton College with bassist Mitchell Player. Welcome to the north. I’m wondering, what’s the temperature in New Orleans right now?
Oh, well it’s like maybe 70 degrees, 74 degrees, something like that.
I could tell you’re not quite as comfortable as your wife in this particular area.
Uh no. I need gloves, wader boots, I mean she doesn’t need the scarf.
But you were up here a number of years ago, after Katrina, so there’s some familiar parts to the scene.

Right, right. I came up after Hurricane Katrina and served as the principal for the YMCA Center for the Creative Arts, which was an afterschool program for kids in Rome and Oneida and exposed a lot of kids to jazz music. Yeah it was quite an experience, you know. I came up here after the devastation of Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans, which is where I was living at the time.
Did you have to leave?

Yeah. I mean I think so. You know, after the storm, and even when the city was officially back up and running, there wasn’t much work for musicians at the time, you know, because there weren’t very many tourists coming to the city. And most people know that

in New Orleans it’s I think mostly the economy is based on tourism. And so yeah, I had to try to find an alternate, some other things to do. I was doing some touring, on the road and everything, and that was mostly when there was a lot of publicity about the hurricane. I mean people obviously were doing what they could to help people from New Orleans in other parts of the country. So there were a lot of musical engagements and performances to help raise money and funds for victims of Hurricane Katrina. And so I did a lot of that touring right after thing — and when it got down in the media so did those gigs, so I was kind of just staying — I went back up and had a place a little north, northwest of Baton Rogue, it was in the country, it was my grandparents’ place, and I was staying there. That’s when my friend Hank Leo called me up and asked me what was going on with me and if I’d be interested in coming up and working with the Y, with the music program with the kids here.

Yesterday you played in Utica. And I was wondering, because both you and your drummer were talking about how joyful and active this New Orleans music is. And is it different to perform for an audience that maybe isn’t as engaged as an audience in New Orleans might be?

Yeah. I think it’s always good for us if the audience is engaged. You know we feed off of that energy. In New Orleans that’s very common when you’re performing or if it’s a parade, or whatever it is, when — it’s like Gerald was speaking about call and response in the music yesterday. When something is done, somebody else takes up where that’s left off. And it’s always a conversation. If it’s the music, or if you ever watched a second line dancers dancing, you know if you see one person doing one dance, then someone else takes over and starts right where that person left off, for lack of a better way to explain it. Yeah. So it’s important for us when the audience is engaged and we’re getting that feedback from them. If we see them moving around, you know, we know that we’re moving their spirit and that’s what we intend to do. The reciprocal of that is then it moves us as well.
Yeah. I think you talked about having — that New Orleans music can mean something different to everybody. You had to make your own connection to it somehow.

Yeah. I think that that’s very much, for me, and I think I find personally for other people that come to New Orleans, or people that I know that already live in New Orleans, it’s New Orleans, it’s so unique and so special for everyone. It’s an individual thing. And I think that’s what always makes the city itself so unique. But then as a result of that, a byproduct of that is that’s the way the people are there. And that’s the way the people have been. And that’s why New Orleans music, the early music, was such an individualized thing. You know when you heard those early traditional New Orleans jazz musicians play, they all were very much individuals. When you go back and you listen to

those recordings you hear the uniqueness in each one of their playing — their sound, their tone — they all had individuality in their playing. And I think that’s the way it is in the city. You know you get there and it affects you and it helps you to realize who you are individually there.

Jazz historians, when you’re talking about that exact thing, about their individual sound, they sometimes say that they were rebelling against the more straightforward European approach to music. Do you think that’s true?

I don’t think that it was a rebellion against — I don’t think it was a rebellion at all. I think it was just, as I said before, just an extension of themselves. I think that because of the unique individual, the uniqueness of everything about New Orleans, the diverse cultures and everything, it allowed people to be individuals. And then that was just as a result of that. They would take that music and, as an older gentleman, a piano player, Lawrence Cotton I played with and he’s like a father to me, he played with Guitar Slim for many years, you know. He said like, “oh, you know, you read a piece of music on paper, but then when you take it off of the paper and you learn it, you make it your own. When it comes out, you make it your own.” You know, you add whatever it is that you want to add to it. And so I don’t think that it was — maybe in some cases, you know, I mean there were times when of course there were musicians who, especially for black musicians in the south, there was a time when there was oppression there, so I guess of course there was, in some ways, people — I don’t know if that’s the best way to describe it is that they were rebelling to make their own music, to make their own way or whatever. But I guess it has a touch of that. But I mean for me it’s mostly about being yourself, being who you are, and that’s part of that whole process.

Well you know, sometimes I think in jazz or in a lot of fields it’s easier to write about things that are negative or that need to be fixed. And recently I’ve been reading articles about jazz and race, jazz and gender, jazz and generations. Is there any issues with that in the current New Orleans music scene?

Oh in the current music scenes? I mean, I don’t really feel that way a lot. I think that we still have racism in our country, and I think maybe for some people, you know, that’s the case. But as far as it being the way it was in the 50’s or the 40’s, you know, I mean musicians play together now, it doesn’t matter you color, if you’re male or female, you know, it’s just about being together and making music. I think there were times when there were laws that would not allow the musicians to play together. I mean that was the big thing for Louis Armstrong. Because he had a mixed band they didn’t want him playing in New Orleans, where he was from, and this was a major issue for him, where he said he didn’t want to come back to New Orleans. But that’s not the case now. Yesterday the 504 Trio was two black males and a young white female, and the band was swinging
and that’s all that matters to us. So I don’t know, I guess that’s different for different people.
Right. Okay. What brought you to New Orleans, and did you decide when you were pretty young that you were going to be a musician?

I did, or at least I started playing music when I was nine. I started playing the bass when I was nine. And I don’t know if at the very beginning I felt like oh this is definitely what I’m going to do for my life, be a musician. But it was probably the primary focus of my life, and just has always been with me. It started at nine, loved playing the bass, started studying classical music and orchestra at school, and then when I got to high school I got introduced to my stage band, and listened to some of my friends’ jazz recordings, and my teacher then introduced us to some jazz recordings. So I got more interested in jazz then. I mean that’s when I kind of started moving more towards saying yeah, I’d like to pursue this a little bit more. So this very good friend of mine, we went to junior high school together and played in bands together at a very young age, is now one of the greatest, I think notable, one of the greatest jazz drummers, Brian Blade. And we went to junior high school together and we played together. And he would come to my house and I would go to his, but he seemed to be — if I ever knew anyone that I thought knew exactly that that’s what they wanted to do, he seemed to be like destined to do what he’s doing today. Even as kids I can remember thinking man, he’s like way out there. But he was, I think it’s a God-given thing. That’s what he was made to do.
Can you remember the first time you made money playing a gig, and how much was it?

I think the first time I actually made money, I think it probably had to be about ninth grade I think. I had already been doing some classical performances, like orchestras and stuff, and my junior high school orchestra teacher had even gotten some of her students who excelled to perform, to do some performances, like pops concerts with the professional symphonies. We’d play with the Marshall Texas Symphony and the Shreveport Symphony early on. But I wasn’t making any money but I was there playing with the other professionals, which was really awesome. It was very meaningful for a kid. But I think when I met my high school band director, Larry Pinell was made I was kind of like going out playing gigs, like when I did something with his band. I don’t know, and I made probably like 70 bucks or something. That was a lot of money. That got me hooked pretty quickly.
That’s 66 more dollars than I made on my first gig.

It was a lot of money. And my parents, they were always very supportive and took me to lessons and everything. So then of course I started playing the gigs, you know, any of the ones that — my parents would go, so that was obviously very good — and be there to make sure — I was underage you know. So there were a few clubs that I performed in

and I shouldn’t have been there, at least legally I shouldn’t have been there, in terms of the age requirement to get in there. But we did all kinds of things. We performed things like debutante balls and weddings and even some club things.
And when were you born?
Okay. So when you were 16, 17, the popular music of the day, did it — how do I say this — did it affect you? Did it pull you away from jazz?

The popular music? I mean I definitely listened to it, like on the radio, a lot. I didn’t necessarily go out and like buy it a lot. I would say that when I did start getting into more like jazz music, if I went to the record store to buy a CD, it was probably jazz. But in high school I listened to Prince and I guess all the other popular bands that all the other kids were listening too. And as a musician I’m sure certainly it had its, it made those impressions on me and part of that comes out in my music because as how we play now, how we interpret the music. But I think a lot of that is environment, what you’re hearing, what your life is like, what the culture around you is like. I mean that’s what I found so fascinating about being in New Orleans, because the culture there is just so different from anyplace else, that obviously has affected me a great deal in how I play, how I interpret the music. Because we live in the heart of the Treme, which is like the oldest African- American community in the U.S. That’s where a lot of the brass band music came out of, early, early on. This neighborhood has been there like 200 years. And I wasn’t living there as a kid. I didn’t grow up there as a kid, but some of my colleagues did, that are New Orleanians, and would tell me about the parades — I mean the parades still go by the houses now. But I can imagine what it must have been like, like in the 70’s, the early 70’s, or mid-70’s. You know, you’d be eight or nine years old and you’d come out and you’d hear trumpets blasting and this group of people, second line going all the way down through your neighborhood. And I mean I get it now as an adult and I joined the second line and, you know, go and find your way a mile away from your house. Because it’s like a hypnotic trance. You know you’re dancing and you’re not thinking about — you know you get a beer from somebody on the way, and you’re not really thinking about just how far am I walking from my house. So then the second line’s over here.
I’ve got to get home.
But yeah, but that music, the style and the music and the people, all of it becomes a part of you. It has become a part of me.
How do you explain to someone who has no idea about the second line — I mean for instance I’ve only seen it on film. And sometimes I’m not sure what that is really all about.

Right. And you know I said this yesterday, speaking about my friend Mark Roe, who said to me once that New Orleans music is a feeling. And he is exactly right. And I think about the city that way. And so I was trying to convey that yesterday when I was speaking to the audience, is that I can try to explain it to you, but I know that I really can’t explain it to you. You have to participate in it. That’s what this music and the city is all about. You have to become engaged in it. And what I find is that I usually, I mostly feel that, I find that people come to New Orleans and they either love it — extremely love it — or they hate it and they feel like it’s the worst place on earth. Now of course everybody is entitled to their own opinion. So that what I always say, come to New Orleans. Come to the Treme and join a second line and feel that and hang out and find yourself two miles from where you started and stopping at a bar here and a bar there and having a drink and friends, and yeah.
You have to let go of your inhibitions, don’t you? To do that?

Yeah. I think so. I think the music is a lot about that, letting go of inhibitions. They have second line parades after funerals. And so — to celebrate peoples’ lives. You know, it’s a celebratory time as well as a mournful time. And the celebration comes after the mourning. But you’re letting go of everything, and you’re just feeling how great it is. But of course that’s individual. It’s an individual thing but it’s a collection thing too, obviously, because you get swept up by things sometimes. It’s such a movement.
Do you think the HBO series “Treme” has done a good job with trying to capture that?

I think they’ve done an excellent job in trying to capture it. It’s the closest thing — and it’s funny because I wasn’t born in New Orleans, it’s interesting when I talk to a lot of my colleagues who, maybe who are New Orleanians, they’re very, very protective in ways, of their culture. So when you see something like the HBO “Treme” series, you know I’ve heard different ones comment like, oh you know, that club — they’re like, when they look at it they’re so meticulous, like oh this club wouldn’t have these chairs there. You know what I mean? Or this wouldn’t be this way. And there have been other shows in the past, series or movie series, or whatever, that have tried to portray New Orleans and they, in my opinion, were terrible. I mean there’s nothing like New Orleans. It’s like that doesn’t even make sense, like the way they move from a shot to some other shot, and they have no continuity. You know, it’s like that’s completely Uptown, and this place is — it just doesn’t make sense what they just did. But the “Treme” series I think is — I mean when I watch it it’s like yeah, this is the real thing. But some people I find, that some people from New Orleans are even more particular about, do they have every single thing exactly like — I mean it’s Hollywood. So that what I think is a disconnect. But I think that “Treme” has done an excellent job. And I think that it’s brought a lot of great
notoriety to the world, Then people can go maybe — it will inspire people to go and check out New Orleans, that maybe never would have before.

I remember seeing a rehearsal scene, and some guitar player got angry or something, and he yanked his thing out of his amp. And someone was smart enough to know, if you yank your — if the amp is on, it’s going to make a sound. And it did. And I said, “now see, a lot of times no one would think of that.”

Exactly. Yeah. And that’s exactly what I mean by, that these people were very, I think, excellent in the recreation of what it would be like in New Orleans. And yeah. So I think they’ve done a great job.
Did they take auditions for people to get in on the thing?

Yeah, you know, I think that they, you know I’m not sure how all of that completely works, but I mean I think that they make posts for like if they need extras for particular shots or whatever. I don’t know what their process is like to get the stars of the show. However, I do know that the main character, he is a New Orleanian, if I understand correctly, and I think he went to the New Orleans Center for the Creative Arts, which is a great school there for high school students. And then the other part is kind of like with jazz gigs, like somebody you know just calls you up and says, “hey man can you do this?” And I mean that’s the way it was for me. You know one of my buddies, a jazz drummer, Gus Johnson, whose passed away now, when I was in the scene that I was in, he called me up and said, “I’ve got this deal in the ‘Treme,’ man, you should come and check it out and be part of it.”

You said something about being protective of the culture. And I was wondering, if I decided I’m going to go to New Orleans and I want to make a living as a musician, what’s it like trying to enter that world and get accepted, and how would I prepare myself?

It’s very open. That’s one great thing about New Orleans, the musicians, the jazz musicians of New Orleans. I think you find that spirit in the south, in Louisiana in general. I hear that all the time. People come to New Orleans and everyone’s so friendly and, you know, people, it’s their first time there and they can’t believe how open people are and how inviting and how friendly they are and how people go, maybe even above and beyond sometimes, to try to be helpful. I hear that a lot. And I think it’s the same way like with the musicians. When new cats come to town they’re always open about letting them sit in, come in and sit in, you know, most of the time, most jazz gigs, most of the band leaders let cats come and sit in, maybe like the last ten minutes of the gig or something like that, or like the last two tunes of the gig. But that’s how you get to know people, you get to hear how they play or whatever. And I mean I guess it depends on what a musician would want to do in terms of if they want to work in New Orleans, as a

functioning working musician in New Orleans, I mean for me I play mostly traditional New Orleans gigs. So that would mean that there’s a certain repertoire, a basic repertoire, that if that’s what you want to do, you should learn those tunes. And then once you know them you just go and sit in. And it’s a great thing, because it gives the bands an opportunity to check out the musicians who maybe want to play, and then it also gives the musicians who want to play an opportunity to check out what level the band is on and if they need to go back home and shed some more or whatever. So it’s good. It’s cool like that.
What’s the average — I don’t know if you can say what an average gig is — what’s the pay scale like in New Orleans? Is it possible to say?

Yeah. I think that the pay generally speaking, and you know, how should I put this, we have a musician’s union in New Orleans. And I could speak for myself. Most of the gigs that I play are in line with what the pay scale is of the union. Yeah. About what the union pays. This is a big, it’s always a big discussion with musicians now, that there was once a time when most of the gigs in New Orleans were union gigs, and the union was very strict about making sure that the union musicians who were performing on those gigs, and they were getting union scale, those days are gone. But what I’ve heard, and I haven’t really done any research about this to really know exactly what the cause of this was, but there was some type of laws that changed, called the Right to Work laws, and I think maybe it was in the late 80’s, something like that. And I mean just generally speaking to other musicians, this is kind of the feedback that I get, and some of them say okay, this is what changed everything for us, and this is when the union no longer had the power that they had.
Yes, I did hear something about that.

So now, so what that meant was then that those club owners were able to start paying musicians, a lot of musicians would either not be union then, of course those musicians would work for less then, so the musicians that were — so that’s difficult. That’s a difficult thing and that’s an ongoing, that’s always an ongoing battle between trying to, if you feel that you’re trying to be at a certain level at your craft and be professional, and then someone who’s hiring you, or hiring that person, will just say well I’ll just get this other person to play for half of what you’re playing. It doesn’t really matter how — I think it’s a lot — if they sound not as good as you, or the band is not as good as you, or whatever. But I think that it’s a lot of different things that contribute to that, I don’t think it’s just one thing, you know what I mean? And what I mean by that is that also now I don’t think our society appreciates music the same way, has a value on music the same way it did in our music tradition, like New Orleans music or jazz music, or whatever, as
they did at a time when maybe musicians were making more, as it relates to the cost of living.
Do you know Evan Christopher?
I do know Evan. He’s very outspoken about it.
Yeah. I’ve been reading some of his things about music and the service industry and all that.

Yeah, he’s very outspoken about it, and rightly so. Because it’s a struggle. I mean if you can think of like I mean this is even really before I moved — I moved to New Orleans in ’94. In the 70’s or something, when all the clubs on Bourbon Street were basically jazz clubs. Now on Bourbon Street there are two jazz clubs. And yeah, two jazz clubs. And there’s one of the, Preservation Hall, or at least clubs that are supposed to be playing traditional jazz clubs or Dixieland or whatever you want to call it. So I mean that says a lot, all those, it’s gone. So now you’ve got karaoke clubs and cover bands and blues clubs, but maybe a lot of that is because that’s what our society now would rather pay to hear, for their entertainment, than it was in the 70’s, when there was more people listening to jazz.

A couple of years ago I attended one of those jazz educator’s conferences, where thousands of people converge on the hotel, and I think it was in New York City. And they had a panel on traditional jazz. And they called it “Trad Jazz, Alive and Well” was the panel. But there was no trad jazz at the festival. They didn’t have any there. They didn’t have any bands performing it. And it was really odd.
Yeah. Right. Exactly. That says it all pretty much. It’s alive and well but where is it?

Well do you have an opinion on why trad jazz and New Orleans jazz and that, it’s so hard to define the stuff, but it doesn’t seem to be taken as seriously as John Coltrane, or Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. There seems to be —

Well I think, yeah, I think mainly right now the reason for that is because what’s promoted as — let’s see I’m trying to say this — the jazz that’s being taught at universities is more like bebop. And I don’t know that, and especially in America — I mean I think back to that whole value system for this music, be it whatever style of jazz, you just don’t have, our society doesn’t value it the way they did, I think, in the past, or as much, or maybe as many people, maybe that’s the better way to say it. And I think that’s as a result of a societal thing. Arts education is being cut in all the schools, and I mean when I was speaking to you earlier about Wallace Davenport, one of the older musicians that I started playing with when I was in the early years in New Orleans, and he played in Basie’s band and Hamp back then. But one of the things he told me one time, I remember him telling me about, he remembered the time when he was a young kid, everybody in New Orleans had a piano in their home. Well you know that doesn’t —

so I mean there was some appreciation in every home, there was some appreciation of music. I mean people appreciated it, even if they weren’t going to be professional musicians, most people maybe had experiences with starting in a band program, or they could at least have some basic understanding to what it would take to become on the level that we know some of our greatest professional musicians are. And so you did have some appreciation there. But now it’s just all sports it seems. And I’m not knocking the football players, but I often think man, if we could just get somebody to go out and market music, market our music the way they market NBA basketball or NFL football. Then we’d be back. Or if there was a way to cross-market those things, then maybe we’d be back.
Is it hard to teach someone to play in the style of a New Orleans musician? What I’m trying to get at is, you mentioned that in colleges it’s like jazz starts with Charlie Parker.
Right.

And they’ve figured out a way, whether we could debate about it or not, they figured out a way to codify what he did, and teach it. But can you codify what a second line is and what those musicians do?

Yeah I think that you can do that in the same way that you could the other styles that they’re doing in the university. I don’t think it’s the same as, like I said, getting the experience on the bandstand. It’s never the same. I mean you can’t get that out of a book, no matter what you’re studying. But when I was in the Y in New York we had a program, I can’t remember the name of it but Wynton Marsalis had put out a great educational program for kids of traditional jazz. And he explained everything. We went through the exercises, explaining like the two-beat feel for the drummer, that marching feel, and that unique New Orleans feel and everything, and traditional jazz tunes, they learned the melody, the chord structure. So it can be done, it’s just a question of the promotion of that. And that’s just not, I mean who makes the decisions on what should be — if Trane should be studied before Louis Armstrong, or why Trane should be studied more than Louis Armstrong — I don’t know who makes, how that comes about. But it’s cool. We just do what we do. And it’s still validating when we’re performing and we see people moving in their seats or who want to get up and dance or want to start clapping on a second line. It means, it’s like Gerald was saying yesterday in our performance, you know we had these little kids who maybe were ten and whatever, and we started playing that “Bourbon Street Parade” with that parade beat, and they were all dancing and moving and shaking. And the teacher was trying to tell them, “no, be still.” You know? And no, the point is for you to move, that’s the whole point.
I know. Doesn’t that make you crazy?
Yeah. And I mean that’s what I mean, yeah. The music is still, it can still move people, it’s just not being promoted to people.

Right. Let me, you just used the term two-beat, and I’m thinking about teaching the bass, teaching young kids how to play the bass, and what their role is. How do you explain those really basic bass things to kids? “No, don’t play four-beat here, play two-beat.”

You know well like playing the bass you could obviously play the walking bass lines, the quarter note bass lines. Or you could, which sometimes when I say oh four-beat, or you could hear a cat say that, or swing out. But then like when you hear the drummer playing and accenting those hits on the bass drum, maybe on two and four [beats] and the bass maybe doing like these — I might actually be playing on one and three but it’s like a [scats]. But the counterpoint of that, all of it, both parts, come from that marching band music that was like reinterpreted as early musicians. Because what happened in New Orleans, I’m not up on all my history, but from what I understand they had some of the military bands that were there that played European style, like the Sousa music, etcetera, and there was no need for the military bands and those instruments of the New Orleanians, brought by people of African descent or whatever, picked those up, and obviously they had been listening to this music by the military bands. So they took a lot of that music and they obviously made it their own. And so that’s where you get this kind of mixture of the marches that they heard, like on “Bourbon Street Parade” you heard Gerald, that tune is traditionally started off with the march sound, the march cadence or whatever, on the snare drum and the bass drum, to lead you into the tune. So yeah, so you just, those things have been taken and mixed and milled together and that’s what you get.
The gumbo.

The gumbo, exactly. You just take it and mix it all up and make something new, and that’s how we get where we are. But it’s very interesting. And I just say to everybody, come to New Orleans. Come to New Orleans and experience it. My wife, Daniella, I met her in Switzerland, and it’s like — you know I often think about that, God, I love her, you know, cause man I don’t know how much longer she can stay. Hopefully she’ll stay. She’s been dropped out from the Swiss Alps.
It’s like another planet.
Right. The Super Bowl in New Orleans. Yeah.
Talk about a change in elevation.

Exactly. Exactly. But she gets it though. She gets it. You know what I mean? Like she’s been there and experiences that she’s had, it doesn’t mean that she loves home any less, obviously, but I mean she loves New Orleans, I know that. And she loves living in the Treme. And she can walk out, she took some of the photos, those were her photos that were run yesterday, and I think she had one of, you know we just had this gentleman,

Uncle Lionel Batiste was a Grand Marshall and a bass drum for the Treme Brass Band. And you know, when he passed away, I don’t know, it was like two weeks that parades went on, because so many people knew him all around the world. I mean they had this funeral, they did a second line, and that huge mass of people that were coming down the street on her photo was in front of our house. It was like opening the door and taking a shot of people. The second line, you know, for his funeral. And again, it’s like I’m sitting here and I’m trying to explain this, but I always feel the same thing, like I’m trying to explain it but I really can’t explain this to people. You know you have to come and experience this for yourself.
Is the current administration in New Orleans supportive? Is it a friend of the music?

You know I’m not really big on politics. I would have to say that — I will just have to say that I always feel like politicians can do more. Because New Orleans is, I feel, the birthplace of jazz music. And like I said before, I can’t understand why you have this unique art form that was created here, and there’s not more that can be done to promote it and preserve it. All of Bourbon Street, there’s hardly no jazz clubs left, you know, traditional jazz clubs. Which is — how many people come to New Orleans and they go to Bourbon Street and they go, “I thought this was where all the jazz was.” No. So I don’t really know how to answer that other than just that I think they could do a lot more to make it — you know there are some great things that happen in New Orleans for the musicians. We have a great — I don’t know how much this has to do with the administration there — but we have a great musician’s clinic. There’s a lot of cases of musicians that come in that don’t have money to be able to pay for their own health insurance. And if there were ways to protect musicians so that they were making reasonable compensation for the jobs that they’re performing I think that the politicians should try to do that. I will say that, from what I’ve heard — I’m not a brass band person — but from what I’ve heard for instance, after Katrina it was a lot harder for brass bands, for instance, to perform in a parade. Like you have to have a permit and you’ve got to pay for a permit. And it probably — so obviously there are probably less parades than happened before Katrina. And that’s a government thing, you know what I mean? They’re supposed to have noise ordinances. If you go down Bourbon Street, it’s so loud. I mean from the Harley Davidsons to the — I mean you know I perform at Preservation Hall regularly and that’s one of the things that’s always irritating to us is that we’re playing all acoustic, no microphone for the vocals to sing, and it’s a great old building, the acoustics are great inside, and the music is great, it’s good. But then you hear that Harley going vroooom. Well it’s a gang of Harleys, not just one. Or the clubs that are sold out, the rock music and other forms of music are so loud that you can hear them there.
What’s the recovery status in New Orleans? Has the city come back?

Yeah, I think the inner city part has. The French Quarter obviously. The Central Business District. Those areas are back up. I think there are a lot of surrounding areas that are still hard hit. People are still — the Ninth Ward, the lower Ninth Ward, out in the east they still have a lot of houses that seem like they either need to be demolished or cleaned up. Somebody should come in and do something about them. So I don’t really know. I think that now we have a lot of new people coming to the city. And I don’t think that that’s necessarily a bad thing. You know, a lot of people who think that it could be — I mean like natives of the city. One thing that happened as a result of Katrina, obviously, is a lot of people moved and didn’t come back. But now you have a lot of new people coming in from all over. People — I guess maybe older people too. But I think that’s what New Orleans always was and always will be — people from everywhere, you know what I mean? So I don’t know that’s necessarily a bad thing. Some people view it as not such a good thing in that it goes back to what I was saying about New Orleanians being so protective of their thing, their place. And I’ve heard on different occasions a native, “where are all these people coming from? Who are they and where are they coming from?” But I think that just New Orleans itself, that it’s always been part of New Orleans, what she is.

The one time my wife and I went was actually shortly before Katrina. And we had that experience of walking, it was somewhere near Bourbon Street, but we could hear this music, and we followed the sound, and on the street corner were these kids playing. And I remember they were doing “Stand by Me,” but they had the — and it was so great. And I don’t know if I was naïve in feeling I’m witnessing something that’s been going on for many, many years, and isn’t it great that it’s still happening. I mean is that a naïve —

No. I think. No, not at all. And I think that that’s again, like — how do I want to describe it — New Orleans, it’s like you see all these progressive things going on maybe, in the city, and then, I mean I think about this from time to time, but then like I’ll go to gigs, week after week after week, and I’m playing songs, obviously we are reinterpreting them over and over and over again, but playing songs from the 1920’s and the 1930’s, the same songs over and over again. So what I mean by that is that the tradition of doing those things over and over again for years and years and years is very much the way things work there. So you have that part where people continue to do — it’s like being in a time warp or whatever, you know what I mean? It’s like you have that part where things are done the same from Topsy Chapman, who is a great vocalist there you know. She and Hank Leo are good friends too, and I was talking to her one day and I was telling her, “oh Hank’s coming down.” “Oh you mention Hank, if he comes to my house I’ll cook a gumbo for him.” You know. But you know, it’s going to take some time because,

you know, you can’t rush good food. You know what I mean? That’s just like the way people are. So yeah, so people just do things the way their mom did them, their grandmothers did them, their grandmother’s grandmother did them. You know. But that’s part of what makes it great too. And so, but then you have people who think that’s like the craziest thing, to keep doing things the same way you would for a hundred years. People are like why would you do that? But then I guess it goes to what your value systems are.
What’s a typical week or month like for you, as a working musician?

Wooo. A typical week? Typical is, right now I’m also working, you know I have a day job because I do it mostly because I have a decent insurance policy, you know, health insurance. So I do that. I work that job, like 30 hours a week, maybe a little more, and then I might do, I don’t know, four or five gigs, three or four gigs a week, and usually a couple of times I’m performing at Preservation Hall jazz club, and then it could vary from private engagements. Like the other day I performed with Dr. Michael White for somebody’s birthday party. You know what I mean? Or I might be performing — they still have a lot of events on riverboats there, like the Natchez Riverboat, or I would perform a lot on the Creole Queen, and then a lot of corporate events that come to town, so those corporate events, for their people, they have performances at the Herman-Grima House, which is a house there in the Quarter that they rent out for special events, catered events, etcetera, etcetera. So, you know, that’s what I’m normally doing. And then of course there are the gigs we get when we go on the road. I still work quite a bit with Leroy Jones and we travel to Brazil quite a bit. You know, before the economy kind of tanked out, we used to travel a lot, in the early 2000’s. That’s how I met my wife, in Switzerland. Every year we would go and perform at the Ascona, Switzerland, the Ascona Jazz and Classics, New Orleans Classics Festival. And so, not only there, we would perform all over Europe. And so that’s how it is for me.
Yeah, I mean it’s similar up here. You get — a gig is a gig.

A gig is a gig. You know sometimes I wish — well I don’t necessarily wish that I’d been there during that time, but I wonder what it would have been like to be there at a time when all those clubs on Bourbon Street were jazz clubs. And when a lot of the older musicians that have since passed on, when they were still alive, living, and what their experiences were like, you know what I mean? I hear stories, but it would have been interesting to see what that would have been like to be around those cats.
Yeah. You know I got to talk with a couple of the guys who had come up here, Kidd Jordan.
Right.
The trumpet —
Clyde Kerr?
Clyde, yeah. And they were talking about some of the studio stuff that went on down there and it was just so fascinating.
Yeah. It’s like it’s endless.
I hope someone invents a time machine someday, so you can go back.
Right. I mean yeah, that would be cool. I don’t know if I’d actually want to be living there, but I’d like to be aware of what’s happening.
Watch Louis Armstrong being arrested on that evening.

Right. Hey what are you doing here? You get in the truck too. You never know. But New Orleans has been great for me personally. My life and my life experiences, like a tear up and I well up when I think about it, like yesterday performing, I was telling my wife, you know, I always forget to bring a handkerchief. Because, you know, when the spirit, with the musicians that I played with yesterday, it’s overwhelming for me, and I’m sure a lot of times for a lot of musicians. It’s such a spiritual thing, or, I don’t know, that’s the best way to describe it. But it’s a very moving thing. And what happens with me is, first the music is moving, and then it all starts going to me like why it’s even happening, like because I made the decision to move to New Orleans, because I played all these years with Leroy Jones and because, you know, then you start thinking about the things like with Sandy of course, that brought all the memories of Katrina back. And all of these things, oh I’ve traveled the world, and how can I have a life like this? I haven’t made a lot of money but man, my life is so rich. I mean, you know, it’s overwhelming for me. So I start crying. I was crying yesterday. That was like, I don’t know I was trying to figure out if I was going to be able to sing. Because my nose was running. I didn’t have a handkerchief, I always forget. Because it’s really great. It’s really been great. And then you know, to come here, and have all of these friends meet you, as a result of, just cause I can play music? You know? New Orleans music? It’s something special. It’s really special. And I can feel it and I can say it, but I can’t make anybody else feel it. I know what I feel.

That was a great thing you just said. I really enjoyed hearing you say it. And it’s interesting too, sometimes you make an impression on young people too, that you don’t know you’re doing it. And I’ve had instances around here, like 25, 30 years later, some adult comes up to me and says, “do you remember that time,” and there were some kids yesterday who was really — and so you just never know.

I talked this morning to Hank, and that’s what I said to him this morning. You know he was getting up, getting ready to go to work, and I was up having some coffee, I woke up early this morning. And while he was going on, he said, “was everything okay yesterday? How did you feel about it?” “Oh, it was great.” It was like, “did you see those kids

dancing and moving around?” I said, “yeah, man.” I said, “that’s Louis Armstrong right there.” You know, because, and the reason why say it is because he was saying this particular group of kids were like from, there were some kids that were supposed to be like troubled kids or something like that, I’m not sure about that. And I told him, I said, “oh yeah, put a horn in their hand.” But that’s how it starts, you know. I was an average student in school. I mean I probably could have done a lot better — I’m more interested in studying now, as an adult, than I was as a kid. But for playing the bass, that’s all I wanted to do. You know, just let me play bass. And so when I think about the fact that, yeah I probably could have been a doctor or a lawyer or a dentist, or, you know, I could have been whatever. I’m very appreciative that my life is what it is. And that I started playing the bass at nine, and thank God I had parents that were interested, but not all kids have that, but that have some role model in their lives that helps them just kind of guide them and direct them until they can get to that place where they feel confident in what they’re doing, you know what I mean? Then they can take it from there. And I think that’s kind of what happened with me, is that I just started with the bass and I just never stopped. And I don’t consider myself the greatest bassist in the world, you know. I mean my idol was Ray Brown. I still listen to him and I hear his sound and go wow man, I try to play like that. But I know I’ve still got time. I still can study. I can still hack away at it as long as I’m here. And that’s like a beautiful thing. But I could have also, like, if I didn’t have that, what would I have been doing now? If I didn’t have music or didn’t have the bass, I don’t know. I don’t think I would have been a rocket scientist, I don’t think that would have been my direction.
In my opinion, the bass is the most important instrument.
Yes.
I mean when you think about it, you can have a band without a drummer. You might not want to, but you can. There has been a number of very famous groups — Nat King Cole.
That’s true, yeah.
But you can’t have a band with a drummer and no bass. I mean you can, okay, the Benny Goodman Trio. But don’t you feel it misses?
Yeah, right.
And I’ve always felt like, man, a bass player, he’s got to be the timekeeper and he’s got to know the chords too.
Right. Just kind of the glue. Just kind of holds it together. Yeah. It’s a team effort. It’s a team. And it’s kind of nice when you’re working with other cats that feel that way too.
Just to wrap up, do you have any fond memories of playing or recording or whatever, with any of the other notable New Orleans fellas, ladies?

Oh there’s so many great memories. I really enjoyed my time working with Wallace Davenport. I was speaking about him earlier. And I think I probably joined that band about ’96 I think, yeah, it was around ’96. And at that time he had a regular engagement at the Maison Bourbon Jazz Club. And all of these gentleman that I played with at that time, they were much older men. That band was Wallace Davenport; Ralph Johnson, who played tenor and saxophone and clarinet; Joe Smith, Joseph Smith, we called him Joe Fox, played drums, he was the brother of Lee Diamond, who you may have heard of, that wrote “Tell it Like it is”; and Lawrence “King” Cotton, who’s now 82, 83, and he played for many years, or for a few years on the road with Guitar Slim and a host of other musicians. It was really an experience to play with those guys and hear the stories that they told about that era, you know, when they were coming through. And Joe Fox had stories about, you know, James Brown. I can’t explain how Mr. Cotton was telling me about like when they would play at the Apollo. And it’s like, “yeah, you know, we’d sleep — we’d take naps — they’d have little bunks in the back and you could lay down and just kind of relax on the bunk, and then the red light would go off in the room and then you’d know it’s time for you to hop up and go on stage at the Apollo.” And Joe Fox told me about James Brown coming to his house, and he thought he was like a little ugly woman. He told his brother, “you better get that little ugly woman out of here before mom gets here.” Man it’s James Brown. These stories. And Wallace would talk about — Wallace told me about the time he was in the Lionel Hampton Band. He joined the Hampton band — this is great. He joined the Lionel Hampton Band. And when I first started playing in his band, it was the same way. He called me the “new boy.” He didn’t call me by name, just the “new boy.” “Where’s the new boy?” That’s what he’d say to all the other guys. And that’s what they’d do in Hamp’s band when a new cat would join the band, they just called him the “new boy.” And so he told me this story about, you know when he was early on in Hampton’s band and there was this guy, I don’t know if he was like the tour manager or something — I don’t think he was actually a musician, but he was always with the band. But he was kind of like a bully, you know. And so he was, I don’t know what he was doing to Wallace, but he upset Wallace. So what Wallace did was, they were out on the road somewhere and he got to a hotel, and when they got to the hotel, Wallace took some talcum powder and put it across the threshold of the door. And being from New Orleans, the guy thought well it’s voodoo, right? So he didn’t want to come out of his room, you know. He came out and saw all the powder on the door. But you know, I mean it was many stories like that with these guys. Many stories. Wow, man, it was great. So that was — so many great lasting — and then I made a lot of stories myself going on the road with our guys, to start off early and get that, it’s like what do
you call it, when you’re passing through, and you’re passing the torch and you’re coming of age. You know what I mean? It’s like this whole thing.
That is great, to watch those guys, how they operate in the clubs and have a taste, and the whole scene is just terrific.
Yeah man, it’s great man, it’s a great life. If people only knew. If they only knew what they’re missing. Man.
Well this has been great. You know, you lifted my spirits today, really. Thank you for being an evangelist for New Orleans.
Yeah. It’s all about the 504.
Right. Thanks for your time.
Thank you, Monk. Thank you man, Thank you very much for having me.

segments.title: Opening and copyright notice
segments.summary: Boilerplate, biographical note and Monk Rowe's welcome.

segments.title: Weather and why Player left New Orleans after Katrina
segments.summary: Small talk about New Orleans weather, then Player explains he left after Katrina because tourism and musician work collapsed.

segments.title: Touring benefits and the call from Hank Leo to teach in Rome, NY
segments.summary: After Katrina he toured benefit shows, stayed at his grandparents' place near Baton Rouge, and Hank Leo invited him to work with the YMCA music program.

segments.title: Performing for engaged audiences and call and response
segments.summary: Audience energy and call and response in New Orleans music and second line dancing.

segments.title: New Orleans music as individual expression
segments.summary: Each person makes a personal connection to the city; early traditional players were individualists.

segments.title: Was early jazz a rebellion against European music?
segments.summary: Player says it was self-expression, citing Lawrence Cotton on making written music your own.

segments.title: Race and the current New Orleans music scene
segments.summary: Racism persists but musicians play together now; Louis Armstrong's mixed band was once barred in New Orleans.

segments.title: Starting bass at nine and friend Brian Blade
segments.summary: Began bass at nine, classical orchestra then jazz in high school; junior high friend Brian Blade.

segments.title: First paid gig and supportive parents
segments.summary: Playing pops concerts with symphonies, then his first pay of about $70 with high school band director; parents chaperoned underage gigs. Born 1970.

segments.title: Popular music, the Treme and the second line
segments.summary: Listened to Prince in high school; living in the Treme and the hypnotic pull of the second line.

segments.title: Explaining the second line: a feeling you must join
segments.summary: New Orleans music is a feeling; you have to participate, and funeral second lines celebrate after mourning.

segments.title: The HBO series Treme
segments.summary: Player praises the show's authenticity, and Rowe tells of a realistic amp detail.

segments.title: Casting and how Player got into Treme
segments.summary: How extras and stars are chosen; drummer Gus Johnson called Player to be part of it.

segments.title: Breaking into the New Orleans scene and sitting in
segments.summary: The scene is open; newcomers sit in and should learn the basic traditional repertoire.

segments.title: Pay scale, the union and Right to Work
segments.summary: Gigs follow union scale, but the union lost power after Right to Work laws; society values music less.

segments.title: Evan Christopher and the decline of Bourbon Street jazz clubs
segments.summary: Evan Christopher speaks out; Player moved to New Orleans in 1994 and notes few jazz clubs remain on Bourbon Street.

segments.title: Why trad jazz is neglected: universities and arts education
segments.summary: Trad jazz panel without trad jazz; universities teach bebop; Wallace Davenport recalled a piano in every home.

segments.title: Teaching New Orleans style and Wynton Marsalis's program
segments.summary: Traditional jazz can be codified and taught; kids danced to Bourbon Street Parade at yesterday's show.

segments.title: Two-beat bass and the marching band roots
segments.summary: Explaining two-beat and four-beat bass and how military band marches fed into New Orleans music.

segments.title: Wife Daniella and Uncle Lionel Batiste's funeral
segments.summary: Player met his wife Daniella in Switzerland; her photos of Lionel Batiste's second line funeral outside their house.

segments.title: City government, preservation and noise
segments.summary: Politicians could do more to promote the music, musicians' clinic, parade permits and Bourbon Street noise.

segments.title: Post-Katrina recovery and tradition in New Orleans
segments.summary: Recovery is uneven, newcomers arriving, and the city doing things as they always were, with Topsy Chapman and Hank Leo.

segments.title: A typical week as a working musician
segments.summary: Day job for insurance, gigs at Preservation Hall, boats and events, touring with Leroy Jones to Europe and Brazil, meeting wife in Ascona.

segments.title: Wishing to have seen the older Bourbon Street era
segments.summary: Wondering what it was like when clubs were jazz clubs; Rowe mentions Kidd Jordan and Clyde Kerr and studio stories.

segments.title: Moved to tears by playing New Orleans music
segments.summary: Overwhelmed by yesterday's performance and the richness of his life in music.

segments.title: Reaching kids, being an average student, and idol Ray Brown
segments.summary: Kids dancing as Louis Armstrong, devotion to bass since nine, and Ray Brown as his idol.

segments.title: Importance of the bass
segments.summary: Rowe and Player agree the bass is the glue and timekeeper of a band.

segments.title: Playing with Wallace Davenport's band and its stories
segments.summary: In the mid-1990s band at Maison Bourbon with older musicians, hearing tales of Guitar Slim, James Brown, the Apollo and Lionel Hampton's band.

segments.summary: Closing remarks and thanks.
